cards.deploy: A portable fairness test for any institution or policy: would you accept it not knowing your place in it?
cards.counter: Nozick and others reject the setup: why assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse (favouring the worst-off) rather than gambling on the average?

cards.title: The median voter theorem
cards.fact: In a simple two-way majority vote, the middle voter decides — so parties drift to the centre.
cards.detail: If opinion lines up on one axis and the winner needs a majority, the option preferred by the median voter beats all others. Candidates converge toward that voter to win.
cards.deploy: Explains why rival parties can end up sounding alike — a clean model for centrist convergence.
cards.counter: It assumes one dimension, two options, and full turnout. Primaries, multidimensional issues, and abstention routinely break it.

cards.title: Duverger's law
cards.fact: Winner-take-all elections tend to produce two big parties; proportional systems produce many.
cards.detail: Under first-past-the-post, votes for small parties are 'wasted', so voters and donors consolidate around two contenders. Proportional representation rewards smaller parties, so more survive.
cards.deploy: Shows that party systems are shaped by the voting rules, not just by the electorate's views — institutions matter.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not an iron law: the UK and India sustain strong regional/third parties under the same rules.

cards.title: The collective action problem
cards.fact: Even when everyone would benefit, large groups often fail to act — because each person can free-ride.
cards.detail: Olson (1965): if you'll get the benefit whether or not you contribute, the rational move is to let others do the work. So big diffuse groups under-organise while small concentrated interests punch above their weight.
cards.deploy: Explains why concentrated lobbies beat diffuse majorities, and why obvious public goods get under-provided.
cards.counter: Selective incentives, social pressure, leadership, and repeated interaction (Ostrom) routinely overcome free-riding — it's a hurdle, not a wall.

cards.title: What economics is about
cards.fact: Economics starts from one awkward fact: we have unlimited wants and limited means.
cards.detail: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people and societies handle those trade-offs — and the cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up (its opportunity cost).
cards.deploy: Reframes almost any policy fight as 'what are we giving up?' rather than just 'is this nice?'.
cards.counter: The scarcity frame can hide questions of power and distribution — who decides what's scarce, and for whom.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: The best alternative you gave up

quiz.q: Economics begins from the problem of…

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.fact: In the basic model, price isn't set by cost or fairness — it's where supply meets demand.
cards.detail: When price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; the price settles where the two meet. It's a powerful starting model — but it assumes competition, good information and flexible prices that real markets often lack.
cards.deploy: Explains why price caps tend to cause shortages and why some subsidies just push prices up.
cards.counter: Perfect competition is rare; with market power, information gaps or sticky prices the simple model can mislead.

quiz.q: In the basic model, the market price settles where…

cards.title: What GDP measures
cards.fact: GDP measures the money value of what a country produces — and quietly leaves a lot out.
cards.detail: GDP totals the market value of a country's output. It misses unpaid work, ignores distribution, and treats some harms as gains — which is why 'growth' is one of economics' biggest arguments.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'the economy grew, so we're better off' — ask what the number counts and what it omits.
cards.counter: For all its flaws, GDP tracks real things — jobs, output, tax revenue — and no rival measure has cleanly replaced it.

quiz.q: GDP does NOT directly count…

cards.title: Why 'political economy'?
cards.fact: Before it was 'economics', it was 'political economy' — and the politics never really left.
cards.detail: The classical writers studied 'political economy' — wealth and its distribution between classes. Around 1900 the field rebranded as 'economics' on the model of physics, pushing power to the margins; 'political economy' names the traditions that keep it central.
cards.deploy: Reminds an opponent that 'just the economics' is rarely just the economics.
cards.counter: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be studied with evidence.

cards.title: The rival schools
cards.fact: There is no single 'economics' — there are rival schools that disagree about how the economy works.
cards.detail: Economics is plural: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural and ecological schools give different answers to the same questions. The mainstream is one paradigm among several, not the last word.
cards.deploy: Whenever someone says 'economists agree', ask which economists — the field is plural.
cards.counter: Pluralism can tip into 'anything goes'; some claims really are better supported by the evidence than others.

cards.title: Adam Smith and the invisible hand
cards.fact: Smith argued a butcher feeds you not from kindness but from self-interest — and somehow it works.
cards.detail: Smith (1776) argued self-interested exchange, coordinated 'as if by an invisible hand', can benefit all, powered by the division of labour. But he also rooted society in sympathy and distrusted merchants — he's far more nuanced than the caricature.
cards.deploy: Useful against caricatures of 'capitalism = greed is good' — even Smith didn't say that.
cards.counter: Smith still defended self-interest and markets as broadly benign — he isn't the proto-socialist some make him either.

quiz.q: Smith's 'invisible hand' is the idea that…

cards.title: The division of labour
cards.fact: Smith watched a pin factory and saw the secret of modern wealth: split the job up.
cards.detail: Splitting work into specialised steps multiplies output — Smith's pin factory is the classic example. But he and later Marx warned it can also deskill and alienate the worker.
cards.deploy: Explains assembly lines, supply chains and outsourcing — and their human downside.
cards.counter: Specialisation also lifted billions out of subsistence; the gains are real, not just the costs.

cards.title: Ricardo and the logic machine
cards.fact: David Ricardo turned economics into a machine of pure logic — and reached unsettling conclusions.
cards.detail: Ricardo built ruthless logical models: comparative advantage, the theory of rent (landlords gain as population grows), and a labour theory of value later taken up by Marx and dropped by the mainstream.
cards.deploy: Shows distribution-as-class-conflict has deep roots inside classical economics, not just in Marx.
cards.counter: The labour theory of value faces hard problems (capital, time, skill) that marginalism was designed to solve.

cards.title: Where does value come from?
cards.fact: Is a thing valuable because of the work in it, or because of how much you want it?
cards.detail: Classical economists and Marx located value in labour; marginalists from the 1870s relocated it in usefulness at the margin. The mainstream took the second path — but the first still frames profit as extraction rather than reward.
cards.deploy: Lets you locate an argument: profit-as-reward (marginalist) vs profit-as-extraction (Marxian).
cards.counter: Marginalism resolved real puzzles — like why water is cheap and diamonds dear — that the labour theory struggled with.

cards.title: The marginal revolution (1870s)
cards.fact: In the 1870s economics quietly changed its mind about what value even is.
cards.detail: Around 1871–1874, Jevons, Menger and Walras relocated value in marginal utility, founding neoclassical economics and shifting the field from class and distribution toward individual optimisation and equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Explains why mainstream economics talks about utility and equilibrium rather than class.
cards.counter: The marginalist tools genuinely unified price theory and remain the workhorse of applied economics.

cards.title: Marx's Capital
cards.fact: Marx didn't just dislike capitalism — he tried to reverse-engineer its hidden machinery.
cards.detail: Marx (1867) argued workers produce more value than their wage ('surplus value'), the source of profit and capital; competition drives accumulation, crises and concentration. His critique outlived his failed predictions.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for arguments about exploitation, inequality and recurring financial crises.
cards.counter: Where Marxist regimes took power, central planning produced its own shortages and repression — the cure has a grim record too.

quiz.q: For Marx, profit ('surplus value') comes from…
choices: Value workers produce above their wage

cards.title: Historical materialism
cards.fact: Marx's big bet: to understand history, follow how people make their living.
cards.detail: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes a society's politics and ideas, and that history advances as productive forces outgrow old ownership arrangements. Powerful as a habit of analysis, contested as a law of history.
cards.deploy: Prompts the sharp question: 'whose material interests does this idea serve?'.
cards.counter: Culture, religion and ideas have driven huge changes no economic base predicted.

cards.title: Keynes and the stuck economy
cards.fact: Keynes argued a market economy can get stuck in a slump — and just sit there.
cards.detail: Keynes (1936) argued economies can settle below full employment when demand collapses, so government should boost demand in slumps. Dominant until 1970s stagflation, revived after 2008.
cards.deploy: The canonical case for stimulus in a recession — private demand can fail to recover by itself.
cards.counter: Sustained deficit spending can stoke inflation and debt; the 1970s showed demand management has limits.

quiz.q: Keynes argued that in a slump, the economy…
choices: Can stay stuck below full employment

quiz.q: Keynes's prescription for a demand-deficient slump was…
choices: Cut public spending to balance the budget
Government spending to lift aggregate demand
Wait for wages to fall on their own

cards.title: The paradox of thrift
cards.fact: If everyone saves more at once, the country can end up saving less.
cards.detail: Saving is prudent for one household but, if everyone does it at once in a slump, spending and incomes fall and total saving can drop — a 'fallacy of composition' Keynes used to justify stimulus.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'everyone should just budget like a household' fails for a whole economy at once.
cards.counter: In normal times saving does finance investment; the paradox is a slump phenomenon, not a general law.

cards.title: Friedman and monetarism
cards.fact: Milton Friedman's counter-revolution: inflation is always, everywhere, about money.
cards.detail: Friedman argued inflation is fundamentally monetary and government meddling does more harm than good. Strict monetarism failed in practice, but his free-market politics shaped the neoliberal era.
cards.deploy: The standard hawkish case that loose money, not greedy sellers, drives inflation.
cards.counter: The money–inflation link is loose in practice; supply shocks and expectations matter, and central banks abandoned strict monetary targets.

cards.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem
cards.fact: Hayek's argument against central planning: nobody knows enough — but prices do.
cards.detail: Hayek (1945) argued that dispersed knowledge makes central planning impossible, while prices coordinate it automatically — a deep case for markets that critics qualify with externalities, monopoly and information failures.
cards.deploy: The strongest principled argument against detailed central planning — it's a knowledge problem, not just a motivation one.
cards.counter: Prices routinely get externalities, public goods and information gaps wrong, which is why even market economies regulate.

cards.title: The hockey stick
cards.fact: For most of history, ordinary living standards barely moved. Then, around 1800, they exploded.
cards.detail: After millennia of near-flat living standards, sustained growth began with Britain's Industrial Revolution (~1800), lifting output per person many-fold — at an immense early human and environmental cost.
cards.deploy: Anchors any argument about technology and growth — the modern world is a recent, fragile exception.
cards.counter: The early human costs were immense, and the gains spread very unevenly across people and regions.

quiz.q: The 'hockey stick' of economic history refers to…
choices: Living standards flat for millennia then rising sharply

cards.title: Enclosure and the making of workers
cards.fact: Before there were factory workers, common land had to be fenced off — and people pushed into wage labour.
cards.detail: English enclosure (1500s–1800s) privatised common land, creating a wage-dependent workforce — Marx's 'primitive accumulation'. Read either as an efficiency gain or as mass dispossession.
cards.deploy: Reminds us markets in land and labour were created — often by force — not simply 'natural'.
cards.counter: Enclosure also raised food output sharply at a time of rising population; it wasn't pure loss.

cards.title: Bretton Woods and the end of gold
cards.fact: For 27 years the world's money was anchored to gold through the dollar — until one night in 1971 it wasn't.
cards.detail: Bretton Woods (1944) pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar; Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971 and money became pure fiat. Whether money needs a hard anchor is still argued.
cards.deploy: Background for any argument about fiat money, inflation, gold standards or cryptocurrencies.
cards.counter: Gold standards impose harsh discipline that can deepen depressions; 'sound money' has real costs too.

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.fact: The 1930s slump was so deep it rewrote economics — and economists still argue about why.
cards.detail: The 1930s Depression — mass unemployment after the 1929 crash — birthed Keynesianism and the activist state. Its causes (demand collapse, monetary contraction, the gold standard) remain contested.
cards.deploy: Every modern crisis response (2008, 2020) is haunted by 'don't repeat the 1930s'.
cards.counter: There's no settled single cause — demand, money, banking and the gold standard all played a part.

cards.title: The 1970s stagflation
cards.fact: In the 1970s, prices and unemployment rose together — which the textbooks said couldn't happen.
cards.detail: 1970s stagflation — high inflation and unemployment together — broke the simple Phillips curve, discredited naive Keynesianism, and ushered in monetarism and the free-market turn.
cards.deploy: The go-to counter to naive Keynesianism — and the origin story of modern central banking.
cards.counter: Stagflation was driven heavily by oil shocks; it didn't prove demand management is always wrong.

cards.title: The neoliberal turn
cards.fact: Around 1980, the rich world swung from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'.
cards.detail: From ~1980, Thatcher and Reagan drove privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation and weaker unions, drawing on Friedman and Hayek. Credited with taming inflation, blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis.
cards.deploy: Names the framework most current economic arguments are still reacting for or against.
cards.counter: 'Neoliberalism' is a loose label; the period's policies and results varied enormously by country.

cards.title: The 2008 financial crisis
cards.fact: In 2008 the financial system nearly stopped — and the faith that markets police themselves took a beating.
cards.detail: A 2008 mortgage bubble froze global finance and triggered the worst slump since the 1930s. The bailout-and-stimulus response revived Keynes and dented 'efficient markets' faith; its causes and the later austerity remain contested.
cards.deploy: The modern reference point for financial regulation, bailouts and 'too big to fail'.
cards.counter: Causes are contested — reckless private finance, or government distortions and easy money, or both.
